lead: On the Saturday after Pentecost the Epistle speaks of the Spirit writing on human hearts: “you are a letter of Christ... written not with ink but with the Spirit of the living God.” The Gospel of the ten bridesmaids asks whether the lamp of that life is still burning when the bridegroom comes. Today is also the memory of St Rita of Cascia, wife, mother, widow and nun, who kept her lamp lit through great sorrow. The key words are letter, Spirit and oil.

r.h: Written not with ink but with the Spirit
set: Some newcomers in Corinth carried letters of recommendation and compared themselves favourably with Paul. Paul refuses to play that game: his only letter is the community itself. He then compares his ministry with that of Moses, drawing on Exodus 34:29–35, where Moses' face shone after he had spoken with God, so that the people “were afraid to come near him” (Exodus 34:30).
str: vv. 1–3: you are our letter, written by the Spirit on hearts.
vv. 4–6: our competence is from God, who made us ministers of a new covenant.
vv. 7–11: if the old ministry came with glory, much more the ministry of the Spirit.
kw: Christ is the author, Paul the one who prepared and delivered it, the Spirit the ink, and the hearts of the Corinthians the page. Jeremiah promised that God would write his law on hearts (Jeremiah 31:33), and Ezekiel that he would give “a heart of flesh” in place of stone (Ezekiel 36:26).

Paul does not set Scripture against inner feeling. The “letter” is the law written outside us, holy in itself but without power to give the life it commands. The Spirit writes God's will within and gives the strength to live it.
vv: You yourselves are our letter, written on our hearts, to be known and read by all;
A changed community is the best proof of a true ministry. People who never open the Bible can still read the Christians around them.
for the letter kills, but the Spirit gives life.

Not an attack on the Law of Moses, which Paul calls “holy and just and good” (Romans 7:12). On its own a written commandment can show sin but cannot heal it. The Spirit gives the life the commandment points to.
how much more will the ministry of the Spirit come in glory?
Paul does not deny the glory of Sinai; he builds on it. The old covenant had real glory. The new has a glory that lasts.
ch: The Catechism teaches that the New Law is the grace of the Holy Spirit given to the faithful through faith in Christ, a law written within, on the heart (CCC 1965–1966). It does not abolish the Old Law but fulfils and perfects it (CCC 1967–1968). St Thomas Aquinas taught the same: the New Law is chiefly the grace of the Holy Spirit itself (in substance). Paul's reading of Moses' veil (3:12–18) is about how Christians read the Scriptures in Christ, and the Church reads it with deep respect for the Jewish people, to whom “belong the covenants” (Romans 9:4; CCC 839).

r.h: Those who were ready went with him
set: The parable belongs to Jesus' last discourse in Matthew (chapters 24–25), spoken on the Mount of Olives in the days before his Passion. After speaking of his coming at an hour no one knows, he tells three parables of the time of waiting: the bridesmaids, the talents, and the judgement of the nations. Read on the Saturday after Pentecost, the parable takes on a particular colour. In the Bible oil is a sign of the Holy Spirit, who anoints and gives light (CCC 695), and the Epistle has just spoken of the Spirit writing on our hearts.
str: vv. 1–4: ten go out to meet the bridegroom; only five bring oil.
vv. 5–7: all fall asleep; at midnight the cry wakes them.
vv. 8–9: the lamps of the foolish are going out.
vv. 10–12: those who were ready go in; the door is shut.
kw: The word used when a town went out in procession to meet an arriving king or great guest and escort him in. Paul uses it of the Church going out “to meet the Lord” at his coming (1 Thessalonians 4:17). The bridesmaids are a picture of the whole Church.
The word of the whole parable. Readiness is not something added at the last minute. It is what a person has become by the time the cry is heard.
vv: As the bridegroom was delayed, all of them became drowsy and slept.
Matthew's first readers were already living with the delay of the Lord's coming. The parable does not scold them for sleeping. It asks what they carry while they wait.
and those who were ready went with him into the wedding banquet; and the door was shut.
The joy of the feast and the seriousness of the closed door stand in one sentence. The time of preparing is now.
Truly I tell you, I do not know you.
Similar words are spoken to those who said “Lord, Lord” but did not do the Father's will (7:21–23). To be known by the Lord is to have lived with him.
ch: The Second Vatican Council takes up the last verse: since we know neither the day nor the hour, we must, as the Lord advised, watch constantly, so that we may enter with him into the marriage feast (Lumen Gentium 48; CCC 1036). St John Chrysostom saw in the oil the works of mercy, which no one can buy at the last hour (Homilies on Matthew 78, in substance). Such works are not our own achievement. They are the fruit of the Spirit in a life kept close to the Lord, and it is the Spirit who keeps the lamp burning.

qa: Does the shut door mean that God's mercy runs out?

No. God's mercy has no limit while we live, and he “is patient with you, not wanting any to perish” (2 Peter 3:9). The parable warns that the time to receive that mercy is this life. The Church teaches that each person receives his eternal recompense at death, and urges us never to put off conversion (CCC 1021–1022, 1036).
rite: St Rita (about 1381–1457) lived in Umbria in Italy. Married young to a violent husband, she bore it with patience and prayer, and he was later killed. She forgave his killers and prayed that her sons would not take revenge. After their death she entered the Augustinian convent at Cascia. She is honoured as a patron of difficult causes. Her life shows the oil of the wise bridesmaids: love kept burning through long years of sorrow.
study: If someone “read” my life this week as a letter of Christ, what would they learn about him?
Is there a conversion I keep putting off until later? What would it mean to be “ready” today?
